concept.name: Miner
concept.definition: A miner is a network participant in a proof-of-work blockchain that expends computation to find valid block hashes, collecting new coins (block subsidy) and transaction fees in exchange for extending the chain.
concept.intuition: Miners are the bookkeepers of a PoW chain who pay for their write access with electricity instead of collateral.
concept.mechanics: Miners gather transactions into a candidate block and repeatedly hash its header with varying nonces until the hash meets the difficulty target; the first to succeed broadcasts the block and earns the block reward (new issuance plus fees). Difficulty retargets so that, regardless of total hash rate, blocks arrive at a target interval.
concept.failure_modes: Miners controlling a majority of hash rate can censor transactions or execute double-spends; falling coin price with fixed energy costs can force miners offline (miner capitulation), temporarily reducing network security.
concept.misconceptions: Miners do not 'create bitcoins out of nothing' — issuance follows the protocol's fixed schedule, and mining revenue competes away toward energy costs. Mining does not verify your personal transactions faster; it secures the whole chain probabilistically.
concept.example: A Bitcoin miner that finds a valid block currently earns the block subsidy (3.125 BTC after the 2024 halving) plus the fees of all included transactions, roughly every 10 minutes on average across the network.

citations.source: Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (whitepaper)
